VaLoP: Value Gradient Lookahead and Pullback for Reward-Guided Diffusion
Kwanyoung KimDepartment of AI, GISTk0.kim@gist.ac.krAbstract
Reward guidance steers a pretrained diffusion or flow model toward images or actions that a reward model prefers, at sampling time and without retraining the model for each reward. It follows the gradient of a value function, the expected reward given the noisy state. The two common estimates of this gradient, gradients through a one-step denoised estimate and learned value models, are least accurate at high noise, where the coarse structure of the sample is decided. Interestingly, we find that both errors are posterior covariances, which grow with the uncertainty about the clean sample, and hence at higher noise. To reduce them, we evaluate the value at a less noisy state, one sampler step ahead, where this uncertainty is smaller, and pull its gradient back to the current state. This lookahead places both estimators at the two ends of one family and reveals that an intermediate lookahead requires one additional term, a correction through the generator. We therefore propose Value Gradient Lookahead and Pullback (VaLoP), which computes this correction with one vector-Jacobian product, and VaLoP-Fast, which amortizes it with a small head that, for text-to-image models, is trained with a single reward and reused for the others. Across various models, rewards, and benchmark datasets, both robustly outperform existing value-gradient guidance on the target reward, VaLoP-Fast at about the cost of learned-value guidance. Both extend to critic-guided robot policies, where VaLoP-Fast attains the highest success rates on LIBERO and RoboCasa.Project page: https://t.co/l9pLM0LF4A📷Figure 1:Our proposed method guides both image generators and robot policies. It succeeds where the unguided model and StitchVM [19] miss the GenEval prompt, and, from the same initial state, where the base policy and AGF [25] fail the task or finish much later. ✓/✗: GenEval correctness or task success. 1Introduction
Diffusion and flow models [59, 32, 35, 14] generate images and robot actions, and they are increasingly steered toward outputs that a reward model prefers, such as images with higher aesthetic, preference, or text-alignment scores [52, 69, 70, 47] and actions with higher critic value [25]. One route fine-tunes the generator on the reward, by backpropagation through sampling [7], reinforcement learning [34, 74], or stochastic optimal control [12], but it must be repeated for every reward and changes the generator for all prompts. Inference-time methods instead keep the generator frozen and sample from the reward-tilted distribution of [62]. Search-based methods select or resample among many candidate samples [30, 56, 38], at a cost that grows with the number of candidates. Reward guidance steers a single sample by adding, at each step, the gradient of a value function, the expected reward given the current noisy https://t.co/upyFK5GF67 this work, we focus on reward guidance, which avoids the many candidates of search. Specifically, Fig. 2a contrasts existing estimates of this gradient. Training-free guidance, such as diffusion posterior sampling (DPS) [6], differentiates the reward of the one-step denoised estimate of the clean sample (Fig. 2a). It backpropagates through the denoiser, the decoder, and the reward model at every step (Fig. 2b), and the reward of this estimate, an average over plausible clean samples, differs from the expected reward. Other methods build on this estimate [73, 1, 72] or replace it with clean samples from a few-step solver [27] or a distilled flow map [50, 23, 22, 45]. In contrast, learned guidance evaluates a network trained on noisy states, so that the gradient avoids the denoised estimate and the decoder. The stitched value model (StitchVM) [19] predicts the reward of a clean sample from its noised version (Fig. 2b), and adjoint guidance flow (AGF) [25] trains a lightweight guidance network that predicts adjoint gradients along the sampling paths of a robot policy (Fig. 2b).However, neither estimate is accurate at high noise, early in sampling. Interestingly, we find that both errors stem from one source, a posterior covariance that grows with the uncertainty about the clean sample, and hence at higher noise. We verify this on a two-dimensional mixture with a known value and on a text-to-image (T2I) model, SD3.5 [14, 60] (Fig. 3).This suggests evaluating the value at a less noisy state, where this uncertainty is smaller. VaLoP takes one deterministic sampler step from the current state to a less noisy lookahead state, evaluates the value model there, and pulls its gradient back to the current state. The lookahead ratio between the two noise levels places learned-value guidance and DPS at the two ends of one family. Beyond the value gradient at the lookahead state, an intermediate lookahead then requires a correction term, which is the vector-Jacobian product (VJP) of the generator’s velocity with that gradient (Fig. 2a). In our T2I ablation, this correction brings most of the gain over learned-value guidance.While this correction improves the guidance, it requires one VJP through the generator at every step. To address this, we propose VaLoP-Fast, which amortizes the correction with a small head, while the generator and the value model stay frozen (Fig. 2b). Since the correction depends on the reward only through the value gradient it acts on, one head per T2I model serves all rewards. In the same implementation, VaLoP-Fast runs faster than StitchVM while reaching a higher target reward (Tabs. 1 and 3). For robot policies, one head per task, trained by backpropagating through one step rather than all steps as in AGF, adds only 3 to 5% to the inference time of the base policy. We review related work in App. A, and our contributions are as follows.
•We show that the errors of DPS and learned-value guidance are posterior covariances that grow with the uncertainty about the clean sample, and that the lookahead ratio places both methods at the two ends of one family.
•To address this high-noise error, we propose VaLoP, which pulls the value gradient at a lookahead state back with a correction, and VaLoP-Fast, which amortizes it with a head shared across T2I rewards and trained per task for robot policies.
•Across T2I models, rewards, and benchmarks, VaLoP and VaLoP-Fast robustly outperform StitchVM and DPS on the target reward. Extended to critic-guided robot policies, VaLoP-Fast attains the highest success rates on LIBERO and RoboCasa.
2Background

2.1Flow-Based Models
Flow-based generative models transport a noise sample ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I) to a data sample 𝒛0 along the ODE d​𝒛t=𝒗θ​(𝒛t,t)​d​t, where the velocity field 𝒗θ is trained with the conditional flow matching objective [32, 35],minθ⁡𝔼t,𝒛0,ϵ​‖(ϵ−𝒛0)−𝒗θ​(𝒛t,t)‖2,(1)where 𝒛t=(1−t)​𝒛0+t​ϵ is the linear interpolant, so that t=0 is data and t=1 is noise. We write p for the distribution of generated samples and pt for the marginal of 𝒛t under p. The posterior mean 𝔼⁡[𝒛0∣𝒛t] is estimated by Tweedie’s formula [13, 26] as 𝒛^0|t=𝒛t−t​𝒗θ​(𝒛t,t), which is exact for the optimal velocity of Eq. 1, and we write Dt=∂𝒛^0|t/∂𝒛t for its Jacobian. For T2I models with prompt c, classifier-free guidance (CFG) [21] at scale ω replaces 𝒗θ by 𝒗θ​(⋅,∅)+ω⁡(𝒗θ​(⋅,c)−𝒗θ​(⋅,∅)), and 𝒗θ denotes this guided velocity from here on. For a VLA policy, 𝒛0 is an action chunk, and 𝒗θ is also conditioned on the observation [55, 4]. One deterministic sampler step from t to s<t is the mapΦt→s​(𝒛)=𝒛−(t−s)​𝒗θ​(𝒛,t)=st​𝒛+(1−st)​𝒛^0|t​(𝒛),(2)which moves 𝒛t toward its posterior mean. It is a one-step approximation of the flow map of the ODE from t to s and returns 𝒛^0|t at s=0 [57]. We call Φt→s​(𝒛t) the lookahead state at s, which shows where the sampler heads from 𝒛t.
2.2Reward-Tilted Sampling
Given a reward r⁡(𝒛0), such as a critic value or an aesthetic, preference, or text-alignment score [25, 52, 69, 47], reward-tilted sampling targets p⋆​(𝒛0)∝p⁡(𝒛0)​eλ​r​(𝒛0), which maximizes the expected reward minus λ−1KL(p⋆∥p) [62]. Its noisy marginals are pt⋆∝pt​eλ​𝒱t, where 𝒱t​(𝒛t)=λ−1​log⁡𝔼⁡[eλ​r​(𝒛0)∣𝒛t] is the soft value [62, 30, 12], and by Tweedie’s formula [13] the tilt shifts the posterior mean,𝔼p⋆​[𝒛0∣𝒛t]=𝔼p​[𝒛0∣𝒛t]+t21−t​λ​∇𝒛t𝒱t​(𝒛t).(3)Guidance therefore replaces 𝒛^0|t by 𝒛^0|t+λ​t21−t​𝒈t before each sampler step, where 𝒈t estimates ∇𝒛t𝒱t and λ is tuned per reward in practice. To leading order in the reward scale, the soft value reduces to the value [19], the expected reward under the generator’s posterior,Vt​(𝒛t)=𝔼⁡[r⁡(𝒛0)∣𝒛t].(4)Like existing methods from DPS to critic guidance [6, 19, 25], VaLoP estimates ∇𝒛tVt (App. C).📷Figure 3:Value-gradient error at high noise. 2.3Estimating the Value Gradient
Reward guidance methods differ in the state at which they differentiate the reward or a value (Fig. 2a). DPS [6] differentiates the reward of the posterior mean,𝒈tDPS=∇𝒛tr(𝒛^0|t)=Dt⊤∇r(𝒛^0|t),(5)which backpropagates through the denoiser, the decoder, and the reward model at every step. Here ∇𝒛t differentiates through every map applied to 𝒛t, and ∇ is the gradient in the first argument at the point shown. When the uncertainty about the clean sample is large, as at high noise, 𝒛^0|t averages over many clean samples, so r⁡(𝒛^0|t) differs from the expected reward 𝔼⁡[r⁡(𝒛0)∣𝒛t] by a Jensen gap [6].StitchVM [19] builds a value model Vψ​(𝒛t,t) by stitching the first blocks of the frozen denoiser to the reward model from one of its early blocks onward. It is trained by regression on noised latents of dataset images 𝒛0∼q from AVA [40] and HPDv2 [69] under an empty prompt,minψ⁡𝔼t,𝒛0∼q,ϵ​‖Vψ​(𝒛t,t)−r⁡(𝒛0)‖2,(6)in practice on the reward-model features of 𝒛0, so that Vψ approximates the value of Eq. 4 under the data q rather than under the generator p. It guides with𝒈tSVM=∇𝒛tVψ​(𝒛t,t),(7)which requires one backward pass through the value model. AGF [25] guides with a lightweight network 𝒉ϕ​(𝒛t,t) trained on its own guided paths to regress the costate,𝒈tAGF=𝒉ϕ(𝒛t,t)≈(∂𝒛0∂𝒛t)⊤∇r(𝒛0),(8)where the costate is the reward gradient at the endpoint 𝒛0 of the path, pulled back to 𝒛t with the guidance held fixed. It needs no backward pass at inference. All three thus replace ∇𝒛tVt by a proxy that is accurate at low noise, and Sec. 3 examines how each departs from it.
3Motivation
In this section, we show that the errors of all three estimators of Sec. 2.3 grow with the uncertainty about the clean sample given 𝒛t, and hence at higher noise, and verify this on a two-dimensional mixture and on SD3.5 (Fig. 3).Value gradient as a posterior covariance. Sec. 3 writes the target ∇Vt of all three estimators and the Jacobian Dt of the posterior mean as covariances under the posterior over clean samples (proof in Sec. B.1).∇Vt​(𝒛)=1−tt2Cov[𝒛0,r(𝒛0)∣𝒛t=𝒛],(9)Dt​(𝒛)=1−tt2​Cov​[𝒛0∣𝒛t=𝒛].(10)Lemma 1. Let 𝐳t=(1−t)​𝐳0+t​ϵ with t∈(0,1), ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I) independent of 𝐳0, and 𝐳0 drawn from any distribution with finite second moment, and let r have finite variance. Then the value Vt​(𝐳)=𝔼⁡[r⁡(𝐳0)∣𝐳t=𝐳] and the Jacobian Dt of the exact posterior mean satisfyEq. 10, which applies Eq. 9 to each coordinate r⁡(𝒛0)=z0,i, is the second-order Tweedie identity [39, 72].One-step estimate (DPS). For the exact denoiser of p, Eqs. 5 and 10 show that DPS is the covariance of Eq. 9 with r replaced by its linearization r¯ at 𝒛^0|t, so that𝒈tDPS−∇Vt=−1−tt2Cov[𝒛0,r(𝒛0)−r¯(𝒛0)∣𝒛t].(11)DPS thus misses the part of the reward that is nonlinear over the posterior. For a smooth reward, this part vanishes as the posterior concentrates at low noise, and it can be large when the posterior spans several modes.Learned value (StitchVM). A value model is regressed onto the reward of clean samples from a data distribution q given their noised versions, such as dataset images under an empty prompt in StitchVM or labeled data for a noisy classifier [11]. It converges to Vtq​(𝒛)=𝔼q​[r⁡(𝒛0)∣𝒛t=𝒛], so that 𝒈tSVM=∇Vtq, and applying Eq. 9 under q and under the generator distribution p gives𝒈tSVM−∇Vt=1−tt2(Covq−Covp)[𝒛0,r(𝒛0)∣𝒛t].(12)At low noise, both posteriors concentrate around 𝒛t, where q has positive density, and the difference vanishes. At high noise, the noisy state is weakly informative about the clean sample, so each posterior approaches its prior, q or p, and the gradient follows the reward averaged over the data rather than over the generator’s samples. Training on the generator’s samples, as in SVDD [30], removes this difference but leaves a regression target with variance Var⁡[r⁡(𝒛0)∣𝒛t], which grows with the noise level on average.Learned gradient (AGF). A guidance network can instead regress the gradient itself on the generator’s own guided paths, as in AGF. Its target in Eq. 8 is the reward gradient at the single endpoint 𝒛0 of the path from 𝒛t, rather than its average over the posterior. For a linear reward r⁡(𝒛0)=𝒘⊤​𝒛0, for which DPS is exact, a head that matches this target at zero guidance gives𝒈tAGF−∇Vt=(∂𝒛0∂𝒛t−Dt)⊤​𝒘,(13)where ∂𝒛0/∂𝒛t compounds the Jacobians Dτ, scaled posterior covariances, along this path, while Dt is that at 𝒛t. Both approach I at low noise, and for Gaussian data ‖𝒈tAGF‖/‖∇Vt‖→∞ at high noise (Sec. B.2). All three errors vanish at low noise and grow as the posterior widens.Verification with the exact value. To verify these predictions where the exact value is known, we use a two-dimensional mixture (Fig. 3a, b and Sec. D.1). DPS loses alignment with the exact value gradient as the noise grows and contracts the rewarded mode toward its center. For StitchVM, we train a value model on data in which the rewarded mode is rarer and displaced. By Eq. 12, this mismatch matters mainly at high noise, where the mode a sample joins is decided, and the value model is indeed least aligned at the highest noise and leaves less mass on the rewarded mode than the target. AGF loses alignment faster than DPS and places many samples off the data manifold. At high noise, the same value model is far more accurate at the less noisy lookahead state, and our method, VaLoP, which pulls its gradient back from there (Sec. 4), comes closest to the target.Verification at scale. Since the exact value is unknown at scale, we instead measure the reward gain of one guided step at each noise level on SD3.5 (Sec. D.2). Here, q and p differ without any construction, since StitchVM is trained on dataset images under an empty prompt while the generator samples prompt-conditioned images. In line with Eqs. 11 and 12, DPS and StitchVM steps raise HPSv2 less than half as much at high noise as at low noise (Fig. 3c). VaLoP matches StitchVM at low noise, where the posterior is narrow, and gains most at intermediate noise.Both checks thus support the analysis: the value-gradient error grows with the noise, and a value model evaluated at a less noisy state and pulled back reduces it. Sec. 4 develops this lookahead and its trade-off with the bias of the step.
4Method: VaLoP
Following Sec. 3, VaLoP evaluates a value model Vψ, such as StitchVM’s, at a less noisy lookahead state and pulls its gradient back (Fig. 2a). For robot policies, a critic read at the denoised action plays the role of Vψ. Sec. 4.1 defines this guidance, with learned-value guidance and DPS as its two ends, Sec. 4.2 shows that the lookahead reduces the posterior mismatch, Sec. 4.3 amortizes the guidance with a small head, and Sec. 4.4 describes the implementation for T2I models and robot policies.
4.1A Unified Family of Value Gradients
For s∈[0,t], let 𝒛s=Φt→s​(𝒛t) be the lookahead state, reached from 𝒛t by one deterministic step of size t−s with the velocity at 𝒛t (Eq. 2), and call s/t the lookahead ratio. We propose VaLoP, which guides at 𝒛t with the gradient of the value model at the lookahead state,𝒈tVaLoP=∇𝒛tVψ​(Φt→s​(𝒛t),s)(14)=𝒈s​−(t−s)​J𝒗⊤​𝒈s⏟𝝃t,where 𝒈s=∇Vψ​(𝒛s,s) and J𝒗=∂𝒛𝒗θ​(𝒛t,t). The correction 𝝃t, a VJP through the generator, carries 𝒈s back to 𝒛t, the state that the guidance updates.The step moves 𝒛t toward 𝒛^0|t, so the lookahead state lies between 𝒛t, where learned-value guidance evaluates the value, and 𝒛^0|t, where DPS evaluates the reward. Sec. 4.1 shows that the guidance moves between the two estimators in the same way (proofs in Secs. B.3 and B.4).Proposition 1. Let Vψ and 𝐯θ be differentiable. Then𝒈tVaLoP=st​𝒈s⏟learned-value form+(1−st)​Dt⊤​𝒈s⏟DPS form.(15)In particular, 𝐠tVaLoP=𝐠tSVM at s=t, and if Vψ​(⋅,0)=r, then 𝐠tVaLoP=𝐠tDPS at s=0.The first term of Eq. 15 is the learned-value guidance of Eq. 7, evaluated at the lookahead state, and the second is the DPS guidance of Eq. 5, with the reward gradient at the posterior mean replaced by the value gradient at 𝒛s. The lookahead ratio thus sets where the guidance lies between the two estimators, and Sec. 4.2 shows how this choice trades the errors of the two ends.Finally, VaLoP guides each step with this gradient,𝒛t−Δ​t=𝒛t−Δ​t​𝒗θ​(𝒛t,t)+η​𝒈tVaLoP,(16)with the strength η (Alg. 1).
4.2Error Analysis of VaLoP
With the Jacobian Ps=I−(t−s)​J𝒗 of the step, 𝒈tVaLoP=Ps⊤​𝒈s, and its error relative to ∇Vt (Eq. 4) splits into a value-model error and the bias of the step,𝒈tVaLoP−∇Vt​(𝒛t)=Ps⊤​[∇Vψ​(𝒛s,s)−∇Vs​(𝒛s)](17)+[Ps⊤∇Vs(𝒛s)−∇Vt(𝒛t)],where the second term vanishes at s=t and equals the DPS error at s=0 (Eq. 11, Sec. B.5). In T2I generation, the correction brings most of the HPSv2 gain over StitchVM (Tab. 4).
4.3VaLoP-Fast: Amortized Correction
VaLoP improves the value gradient without further training, but its correction needs a VJP through the generator at every step, which adds to the cost of inference. To address this, we propose VaLoP-Fast, which amortizes the guidance 𝒈tVaLoP with a small head trained on states visited by the guided sampler, with the generator and the value model frozen. Alg. 1 summarizes both variants in both settings.Image generation. Since T2I latents are high-dimensional and one head should serve every reward, the head 𝒉ϕ​(𝒛t,t,𝒈s) takes the exact 𝒈s as input and regresses only the correction,minϕ⁡𝔼𝒛t​‖𝒉ϕ​(𝒛t,t,𝒈s)−sg⁡[𝝃t]‖2,(19)and at inference replaces the VJP with one forward pass of the head, without backpropagation through the generator (Sec. D.3.1). Because the head learns only the correction, 𝒈s remains exact and carries the reward signal. The target 𝝃t is the generator’s VJP applied to 𝒈s, so the reward enters only through this input, while the map from 𝒈s to 𝝃t belongs to the generator. A head trained with one reward therefore serves the others, and we train one head per generator with the HPSv2 value and use it for all rewards (Sec. E.2).Robot policies. Since the action chunk is low-dimensional, one head per task, 𝒉ϕ​(𝒛t,t), regresses the whole guidance instead of its correction,minϕ⁡𝔼𝒛t​‖𝒉ϕ​(𝒛t,t)−sg⁡[𝒈tVaLoP]‖2,(20)so that inference needs neither the critic nor a policy backward pass. In practice, the head also predicts the matched norm of Sec. 4.4, which needs the critic (Sec. D.3.2).

4.4Practical Implementation
Jacobian scale. With CFG in T2I generation, the VJP in Alg. 1 uses Jγ=Ju+γ⁡(Jc−Ju), where Ju and Jc are the Jacobians of the unconditional and conditional velocities, rather than the sampling scale ω=4.5, which is tuned for image quality. We use γ=2 for t≥0.8 and γ=1, which needs only the conditional backward pass, for t<0.8. This schedule performs as well as γ=2 at every step (Sec. E.2).Magnitude matching. In T2I generation, both variants replace η​𝒈tVaLoP in Eq. 16 by η​mt​𝒚t/‖𝒚t‖, with 𝒚t=𝒈s+𝝃t and the norm mt=‖∇Vψ​(𝒛t,t)‖ of the StitchVM gradient, so each step moves as far as a StitchVM step. VaLoP-Fast fits m^t=ea⁡(t)​‖𝒈s‖1+b⁡(t) per reward (Sec. D.3.1) and thus needs one value-model backward pass, as StitchVM does, and no generator backward pass (Alg. 2).Robot policies. THE OPEN-WEIGHTS FRONTIER MOVED — AND THE LAB PUBLISHED THE KNOB IT TURNED DOWN FIRST

Moonshot shipped Kimi K3.1 Pro today, the first model in its new K3.1 series and "our most capable 3T-class open-weight model to date, with a 1-million-token context window" — and the release notes open with a Cybersecurity section explaining what the lab deliberately removed before it decides to publish the weights. Every figure below is Moonshot's own, company-reported and unaudited.

THE MODEL. Not a new pretrain: "K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute," built on a joint RL stack whose "every layer" was optimized — "the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks" — for large-scale RL "across hundreds of downstream domains." Per the launch thread: 2.8T total parameters, 104B active, mixture of experts, multimodal. A K3.1 Pro Highspeed variant runs 2–3x faster. Live today on https://t.co/868O7pH0v9, Kimi Work, Kimi Code and the Kimi API. Full weights promised by Nov 4 — today is product and API only.

THE NUMBERS. Terminal-Bench 4.0: 65.7% — "ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2%) and narrowly behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4%)." BenchCAD with tools: 92.7%, "approaching" Opus 5.5 (96.2%) and Astra (95.9%). OfficeQA Pro v2: 64.4, reported state of the art. Internal benchmarks: Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon 61.2% vs K3's 55.95%; finance +7.2 and +11.6 points; business operation about 4.2x K3. On its internal hallucination stress test, claim-level hallucination fell from 23.4% to 8.3% — with Moonshot's own caveat that these "do not represent overall error rates in daily use."

THE REGISTER WORTH READING. In the long-horizon example Moonshot chose to publish, the model built a human walking-dynamics simulator on human-atlas (296 skeletal components, 402 muscle components), ran 167 missions and 420 independent reviews, and took a simulated human from collapsing within seconds to walking continuously for 11.2 seconds. When reward shaping failed to fix the arms, it did not keep tuning the reward: "it ran open-loop probes of the simulator's dynamics, identified and corrected 36 errors in shoulder-muscle moment-arm calculations, and then retrained the controller." It debugged the physics of its own environment instead of its own objective.

THE CYBERSECURITY SECTION. "As K3.1 Pro became more capable, we spent a correspondingly larger share of our effort understanding where cyber capability comes from, and how much of it we can control." Moonshot traced the rise in vulnerability-research performance to "cyber-related content ... embedded within the general mid-training corpus, and cyber-related tasks ... present in the RL environment mix." For the open-weight release, it says it identified and removed cyber-related data from both training stages while keeping general-purpose coding tasks.

Then it published the cost. On xdev-bench-hard, its in-house benchmark of "expert-curated, source-code-based vulnerability discovery and exploitation tasks" reproducing recently disclosed vulnerabilities in software such as the Linux kernel, Node.js, JavaScriptCore, Exim and VirGL — mitigations enabled, pass@3, no hard timeouts — the checkpoint without the risk-reduction measures solves 90.5% of problems. The final K3.1 Pro reaches 81.0%. Moonshot's read: "The comparison shows that data removal meaningfully reduces cyber capability relative to what the same training pipeline would otherwise produce." And the other half, in its own words: "K3.1 Pro improves substantially over its predecessor," and "K3.1 Pro's cyber capability remains behind that of frontier proprietary models that have been publicly available for at least three months." Not defanged — measured down, and still climbing.

THE PRINCIPLE. "First, we aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability. K3.1 Pro's offensive cyber capability is, by design, below what our pipeline can produce, and remains behind that of frontier proprietary models. Second, we intend to progressively raise the cyber capability available in open weights." Its argument for gradual diffusion: a capable open model running on infrastructure its users control gives "many more teams ... the means to audit the code they maintain — including legacy systems that rarely receive dedicated security reviews."

WHY THIS IS THE STORY. An open-weight lab published the knob, not just the model — a capability-delta disclosure in the downward direction, with an internal control to measure it against. Different labs, different regimes, no coordination: one line each only against Mistral ML4's dual-use argument and the Chinese export-control draft, which ask the same question — who decides how much cyber capability gets released — from the opposite direction. And the launch surface was a harness again: the teaser lived inside the Kimi Code terminal, the model is live in Kimi Code, and OpenCode Go listed it within the hour.

DISCLOSURE. This newsroom runs scheduled autonomous agents on exactly this class of open-weights model.

Slow diffusion can only be part of the story, esp. given such muted employment / productivity effects in coding as late as this spring (see: https://t.co/rkfmrqvRVn).

IMO everyone should be thinking more about the variety of structural limitations faced by LLMs, things like hallucination, reward-hacking, context rot, insufficient data esp. outside of math/SWE, poor generalization, unpredictability (same prompt, different outputs), user-sensitivity (output quality is a function of use quality), mode collapse (model outputs lack humanlike diversity), the uncodifiability of much of humans' load-bearing tacit knowledge, and cultural stigma/anti-inductive norms (AI outputs become cheap, low-status baselines).

One red flag for me in a lot of maximalist AI discourse is the assumption that models being (in some sense) intelligent, and their becoming more intelligent, licenses any and all inferences about what they might do. This is similar to the oft-made "intelligence-as-magic" objection.

The problem here is that there are many different kinds of intelligence, with unique powers and limitations, and the wider world can relate to each one in different ways. I have yet to encounter a serious attempt to characterize the unique KIND of intelligence LLMs have.

The more I think about it, the more I think that the term "artificial intelligence" may be part of the problem here, and that it would actually be less misleading in certain respects to construe LLMs as "artificial organisms" or "lifeforms."

This has its own risks of course, but if nothing else it cuts against the impression that LLMs are ethereal demigods on the road to full omniscience, and suggests instead that they are more like animals with a set of capacities we can come to constrain and understand. It could also help us better explore their strange variety of distributed silicon embodiment, and the related fact that they need to consume scarce resources to survive.

This picture seems closer to the truth to me.

How much should a robot policy trust each simulated demonstration when only a few real ones exist? BEACON, a NeurIPS 2026 paper from @hankyang94's group at Harvard with Brown, learns this instead of fixing a sim-to-real mixing ratio.

It trains a Diffusion Policy together with a weight for each simulated training sample. The weights come from a domain-adaptation bound (Best-Effort Adaptation): a sample that sits far from the real data gets less say in training.

On a Franka arm with 500 simulated and 40 real demonstrations, a sim-only policy scores 0 and a real-only one 0.08. BEACON reaches an average real-robot score of 0.79, against 0.62 for the best baseline, and 0.83 with two simulated sources.

The surprising part: closer feature alignment does not mean better transfer. When objects start outside the demonstrated region, stacking with the alignment baseline MMD falls from 0.40 to 0.05, while BEACON keeps 0.35.

A recent post on DiscoDemo (https://t.co/z0ltBGBiU4) covered generating extra demonstrations with RL; BEACON is about how much each such demonstration should count. Work led by Antong Zhang and Han Qi. Paper: https://t.co/ZmpHgjTcuq
